Presenting
Your Findings

Explaining numbers, graphs, and technical information to an audience, in English

Dr. Brandon L. Kramer · Saturday, October 24, 2026 · 2:00–4:00 p.m.

brandon.l.kramer@gmail.com

2:00–2:01. Welcome. Today is about communicating findings, not calculating statistics. Everyone will speak a lot, mostly in pairs.

PracticeIntroductions · everyone

Who are we?

1Name

"I'm ___ from the ___ department / office."

2Your work

"I research ___." / "I work with data on ___."

3One goal

"I'd like to get better at explaining ___."

About 30 seconds each.

2:01–2:07. Go first as the model: "I'm Brandon from Kwansei Gakuin University. I research vocabulary learning and language testing. I'd like to get better at explaining statistics to people outside my field." Note each person's field; use their topics as examples later. Administrative staff: "the data I work with" is fine.

Today's goal

Don't just tell people what the data say. Help them see what to notice and why it matters.

Describe

What does the data show?

Interpret

What might it mean?

So what?

Why does it matter to this audience?

2:121 · Basic statistical information
2:352 · Explaining charts and graphs
3:203 · Explaining technical information
3:40Your 90-second mini-presentation

2:07–2:09. The three parts are the organizer's three areas. Explain the idea: an IELTS-style description stops after "Describe". A good presentation also answers "So what?" Throughout the workshop, listeners will ask "So what?" after every explanation. Break at 3:05.

PracticeCompare two explanations

Both are accurate. Which is easier to follow?

Version A

"Group A had a mean score of 73.4, Group B had 68.2, and the standard deviations were 9.2 and 11.4, respectively."

Version B

"Group A scored about five points higher than Group B. However, scores varied quite a bit within both groups."

  • Why is B easier to follow?
  • What does A contain that a technical audience might still need?
  • Is the difference in the phrasing, the selection, or both?

2:09–2:12 (with the next slide). B gives the comparison and the meaning of the SDs instead of listing them. A's exact values belong in a paper, a table, or the Q&A. The answer: both selection and phrasing.

Key idea

Start with the message, not the numbers

1Message

What should the audience notice?

2Evidence

The numbers that support that message.

3Detail

More precise values, only if this audience needs them.

From the field

Don't read all the numbers. Focus on the important points, and leave the numbers on the screen for those who want the detail.

Link to Version B: message ("Group A scored higher"), evidence ("about five points"), detail (exact means and SDs) held back. Introduce "From the field": tips collected from well-known researchers in applied linguistics. They appear in every part.

With a partner

Message: one sentence. What should the audience notice?
Evidence: one sentence, with the numbers that support it.
"Satisfaction with the library has dropped. This year, 62% of the 200 students we asked were satisfied, down from 70% last year."

Optional, 3 minutes. Several messages are possible ("most students are satisfied" is also accurate). Ask pairs which numbers they left out, and why. Press R for one model.

Part 1 · Basic statistical information

Useful ways to describe numbers

Averages

The average score was 72.

On average, participants scored…

Proportions

Approximately 60% of respondents…

Just over half of the participants…

Just under one third…

Comparisons

Compared with Group B, Group A scored…

The difference was relatively small.

Change

Participation increased from 40% to 55%.

The number fell sharply to…

Caution

The results suggest that…

Saying it aloud

54.2 fifty-four point two

115,146 about a hundred and fifteen thousand

2:12–2:15. Read a few aloud; participants repeat. Keep it short: a small set of reliable phrases. Pronunciation: stress on fif-TEEN vs. FIF-ty. Large numbers: 1万 = ten thousand, 10万 = a hundred thousand.

Say three sentences

Before 2020, about students studied abroad each year.

Round the numbers when you speak.

2:19–2:22. Model: "Before 2020, about a hundred thousand Japanese students studied abroad each year. In 2020, the number fell sharply to fewer than fifteen hundred. By 2024, it had recovered to just over ninety thousand." So what? "Study abroad has almost recovered, but it's still below the level before the pandemic."

Part 1 · Staying accurate

66% → 92%

A 26-percentage-point increase

92 − 66 = 26

An increase of about 39%

26 ÷ 66 ≈ 0.39

Both are true. Say which one you mean.

2:22–2:24. Ask: "If you wanted the change to sound bigger, which would you choose?" From 92% to 95% is 3 points: "AI use has leveled off near the top."

Which version would you use in a presentation? Why?

2:24–2:26. Pairs take turns saying each row both ways. Press R to check. Rows 1 and 2 have the same point change but very different percent changes. Row 4 is the "doubled!" headline problem again.

Part 1 · From the field

Always give the denominator

"13 of our students entered the University of Tokyo!"

A typical cram school advertisement. Out of how many?

13 out of 40 students

33%

13 out of 2,000 students

0.65%

From the field

Give percentages, so the audience has some perspective on what the numbers mean. And say how many people the numbers are based on: "1,054 respondents".

2:26–2:28. Same count, very different meaning. Point back to the AI chart: its note gives the denominator (1,054 respondents). Phrases: "13 out of 40", "about a third of", "fewer than 1 in 100".

PracticePart 1 · Pair task · Say it more naturally

Rewrite each statement, then say it aloud

OriginalA more natural version
"The participants of 54.2 percent are answering yes.""Just over half of the participants answered yes."
"The mean of satisfaction score was 3.87 in 5-point scale.""On average, satisfaction was just under 4 out of 5."
"Group A is 71.6 and Group B is 68.9 for the score.""Group A scored about three points higher than Group B."
"312 people from 1,040 people did respond.""About three in ten people responded: 312 out of 1,040."

2:28–2:35. Model row 1. Pairs work on rows 2–5 and say them aloud. Press R to reveal. Row 5: the natural version gives the denominator and a percentage. After each answer, a partner asks: "So what?"

PracticeOptionalPart 1 · Your own number

Say one number from your own work

Part 2 · Explaining charts and graphs

Four moves, then "So what?"

1Introduce

"This graph shows…"

2Orient

"The horizontal axis shows…"
"Each line is…"

3Highlight

"Look at… The main pattern is…"

4Interpret

"This suggests that…"

5So what?

"In plain terms, this means…"

IELTS Task 1

Overview, key features, comparisons. Stops after describing.

A presentation

Also tells the audience where to look and why it matters.

2:35–2:38. Many participants know IELTS-style graph descriptions. They are a good start: accurate, organized, overview first. A presentation adds pointing ("look at…") and the so-what.

Part 2 · Demonstration · Written vs. spoken

Written"Reading showed the greatest fluctuation, increasing from 498 points to a peak of 538 before dropping to 504 in 2018 and recovering to 516."

Highlight"Look at the orange dashed line. That's reading. It went up and down much more than the other two subjects."

Caution"Note that the axis starts at 490, so these changes look bigger than they are."

So what?"In plain terms, Japan's scores dropped for a few years, but by 2022 they had mostly recovered."

2:38–2:41. The written sentence is from your class model answer: accurate and complete. The spoken version tells people where to look, gives fewer numbers, flags the axis, and ends with a so-what. Ask: which numbers did the spoken version leave out, and why is that acceptable? (They stay on the screen.)

PracticePart 2 · Your turn: four moves + so what

In pairs, 45 seconds each

1 Introduce2 Orient3 Highlight4 Interpret5 So what?

Partner: ask "So what?" if they forget.

2:41–2:45. Model if needed: "This chart shows how UK undergraduates used AI for assessed work. Each bar is one use. Look at the top bar: 61% used it to explain concepts. Only 12% put AI text directly into their work. So what? Most students use AI to understand material, not to write for them." Denominator: 1,054 respondents.

Part 2 · From the field

Guide the audience's eyes

From the field

Tell people where to look on a graph.

From the field

Don't make slides too busy.

From the field

If presenting in English, try not to read.

Pointing phrases

  • "Look at the line at the top…"
  • "On the right-hand side, you can see…"
  • "The orange bars show…"
  • "Notice the sharp drop in 2020."
  • "Compare these two bars."

2:45–2:47. Not reading: put only short labels on slides, so there is nothing to read aloud. Your notes can be on paper or in presenter view.

"Compare the two blue bars."

Partner B points to it and says the number. Three directions each, then swap.

Optional, 3 minutes. Partners point at the screen or a printout. Useful words: left / right, top / bottom, the tallest bar, the blue bars, the label.

Part 2 · Charts in scientific presentations

Which chart for which data?

Bar chart

Counts and percentages

Line graph

Change over time

Scatterplot

Relationship between two measures

Boxplot

Scores of groups: the distribution

Most of the charts you've seen today are bar and line charts of percentages and counts. That's a good use. Averages of scores need something else.

2:47–2:49. Connect to their charts: the study-abroad destinations and AI uses are counts and percentages, so bars are fine. Scatterplot = practice chart E; boxplot is next.

2:49–2:51. Pairs decide quickly, then press R. Accept reasonable alternatives (enrollment could be bars), as long as the reason is clear.

Part 2 · From the field · Same data, two charts

Bar + error bar The groups look almost the same.

Boxplot Group A's scores are far more spread out.

From the field

Avoid vertical bar charts with error bars on top. Use charts that show the distribution. A standard boxplot is best: no extra layers, no bright colors.

2:51–2:53. Illustrative data: vocabulary test, out of 20. Averages are 12.0 vs. 12.9. The bars hide that some Group A students did very well and some very poorly. So what? "The method used with Group A may work well for some students but not for others."

Part 2 · How to describe a boxplot
"The line in the box is the median, the middle score."
"The box shows the middle half of the students."
"The lines show the range of most scores."
"The dot is an unusual score."
"Scores in Group A were more spread out."

2:53–2:54. For audiences outside statistics, say "middle half" rather than "interquartile range".

Three sentences + so what

Which class had the highest median?
Which class was most spread out?
Anything unusual?
"Class 2 had the highest middle score, about 6.5 out of 10, and its scores were the most consistent, apart from one unusual low score. Class 3 had the lowest median and the widest spread. So what? Class 3 probably needs the most support."

Team Success

Make study abroad sound like a success story.

Team Crisis

Every sentence must be true. You may choose the years, the numbers, and the verbs.

Honest: "Study abroad collapsed in 2020 and has mostly recovered, to about 91,000 in 2024. That's still below the 2018 peak of about 115,000."

Optional, 6–8 minutes. Success: "Since 2020, study abroad has grown more than sixtyfold." Crisis: "We are still more than 24,000 students below 2018." Both are true. The room names the trick (choosing the start year, percent vs. count, strong verbs), then press R for an honest version.

Part 3 · Explaining technical information and data

Simplify the language, not the meaning

Technical

"A statistically significant interaction was observed between instructional condition and time, indicating differential developmental trajectories."

Accessible

"The two groups changed differently over time. In other words, the difference between the groups depended on when they were tested."

Careful: "the effect of the teaching method" would claim a cause the study may not support.

Illustrative teaching data (chart D)

3:20–3:22. The chart shows what an interaction looks like: the lines cross. Ask pairs to point to the part of the chart each sentence describes. Press R for the caution.

Part 3 · Three tools

Define, rephrase, exemplify

1Define

"By retention, I mean how much people remember later."

2Rephrase

"In other words, the two groups changed differently."

3Exemplify

"For example, imagine a student who studies new words on Monday and is tested a month later."

Your listener's three questions: "What does that mean?" · "Can you give me an example?" · "So what?"

Adapted from Ken Bain, What the Best College Teachers Do (2004)

3:22–3:24. Each tool answers one of the listener's questions: define and rephrase answer "What does that mean?", exemplify answers "Can you give me an example?", and the plain-language takeaway answers "So what?"

PracticePart 3 · Explain it twice

Say it for researchers, then for everyone else

For researchersFor a general audience
"Participants in the treatment condition demonstrated significantly greater gains in productive vocabulary knowledge.""Students who had the new lessons improved more in the words they could actually use."
"Inter-rater reliability was high (κ = .85).""Two teachers scored the essays separately, and they mostly agreed."
"The score distribution was positively skewed.""Most students got low scores; only a few got very high ones."
"The response rate was 38%, so non-response bias is possible.""Only about four in ten people answered, so the results may not represent everyone."

3:24–3:29. Pairs take one row each, explain it in plain English, and the partner asks "What does that mean?" or "Can you give me an example?" Press R for models. Then: "So what?"

PracticePart 3 · Activity · Explain it outside your field

Choose one and explain it

"The survey response rate was 38%."

"There was a weak positive correlation between sleep and exam scores."

"The difference was significant, t(58) = 5.90."

A phrase from your own work

Listener: keep asking

"What does that mean?"
"Can you give me an example?"
"So what?"

3:29–3:34. Models if needed:

  • Response rate: "We sent a survey to a group of people, and 38% answered, about four in ten. The people who answered may not represent everyone."
  • Weak positive correlation: "Students who slept more tended to score a little higher, but many did not. It doesn't show that sleep caused the higher scores." (Chart E.)
  • t-test: "The reading group scored about three points higher out of 20, and that difference is unlikely to be chance. In practical terms…"

Part 3 · From the field

"Significant" is not the same as "important"

The difference is statistically significant. But what is it in practical terms?

"In practical terms, that's about three more words out of twenty."
"For a teacher, this means…"
From the field

Don't overemphasize "it's significant". Many vocabulary studies report a significant difference of about 3 points on a 20-item test.

3:37–3:40. Same illustrative data as the table. Is 3 out of 20 a lot? It depends on what the 20 items represent. The point is to tell the audience the size in everyday terms and let them judge.

PracticeOptionalPart 3 · Big or small?

What does it mean in practical terms?

FindingIn practical terms
"Group A scored 2 points higher on a 50-item test, p < .05.""About 4% of the test. Statistically significant, but a small difference."
"Attendance rose from 82% to 85%.""3 points: in a class of 30, about one more student each lesson."
"App users studied 12 minutes more per week.""Less than two minutes a day."
"In practical terms, that's about…" · "For a teacher / a student, this means…"

Optional, 3–4 minutes. Pairs decide: is it big or small? Then press R. There's no single correct answer; the point is to translate the number into everyday terms.

PracticeOptionalPart 3 · Find the misleading conclusion

Which conclusions does the chart support?

A "Teens with 4+ hours of screen time were more than twice as likely to report anxiety symptoms."

Supported: 27.1% vs. 12.3%.

B "Screen time causes anxiety and depression."

Not supported: an association, not cause.

C "About a quarter of U.S. teens have depression."

Not supported: 25.9% is only the 4+ hours group, and these are symptoms, not diagnoses.

Optional, 4 minutes. Pairs decide and explain why, using "This suggests…" / "We can't say…". Press R for answers.

Practice 2 · 90-second mini-presentation

A framework you can reuse

1"We wanted to investigate…"Purpose
2"This figure shows…"Introduce, orient, where to look
3"The most important finding is…"Highlight, with the denominator
4"One possible explanation is…"Interpret, with caution
5"So what? The key takeaway is…"In plain language

3:40–3:43. Model with the screen-time charts: "The CDC wanted to know how much screen time American teenagers have. This chart shows... Look at the orange bars. Among teens with four or more hours a day, 27% reported anxiety symptoms, compared with 12% of the others. One possible explanation is that heavy screen use affects mental health, but it could also work the other way, and this survey shows only an association. So what? Screen time and mental health are linked, but we shouldn't assume one causes the other."

3:43–3:55. Nobody needs to bring their own data. Two rounds so everyone presents. If time allows, one volunteer presents to the whole room.

Wrap-up

Three final takeaways

1Lead with the message

Tell the audience what to notice, and where to look.

2Use numbers selectively

Keep them accurate, and always give the denominator.

3Answer "So what?"

In the plainest language you can.

Before: "Group A had a mean score of 73.4, Group B had 68.2…"

After: "Group A scored about five points higher than Group B."

3:55–3:58. Return to the opening comparison and the goals from the introductions. Invite participants to apply the framework to one slide from their own work.

From the field · Checklist

Before you present

  • Is my slide too busy?
  • Can I present without reading?
  • Do I tell people where to look?
  • Do I focus on the important numbers, and leave the rest on screen?
  • Did I give the denominator and a percentage?
  • Averages of scores: a boxplot, not bars with error bars?
  • A standard boxplot, without extra layers or bright colors?
  • "Significant" explained in practical terms?
  • A short summary, not a pasted software table?
  • Does every statistics-heavy slide end with a "so what"?

3:58–4:00. This checklist is also on the worksheet. Thank the organizer and participants.
